questions.body: In what order does the JavaScript runtime event loop process tasks?
questions.keyPoints: Execute synchronous stack, drain entire microtask queue, then take one macrotask from task queue.

options.text: Execute call stack -> Drain all microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) -> Execute one macrotask (setTimeout, I/O) -> Repeat.
options.explanation: After synchronous code finishes, the microtask queue is completely drained before rendering or taking the next macrotask from the task queue.

options.text: Execute macrotask -> Execute all microtasks -> Execute call stack.
options.explanation: Synchronous call stack runs first.

options.text: Microtasks and macrotasks run concurrently in parallel threads.
options.explanation: JavaScript main thread execution is single-threaded.

options.text: `setTimeout` tasks have higher priority than Promise `.then()` callbacks.
options.explanation: Promise callbacks are microtasks and have strictly higher priority than `setTimeout` macrotasks.

questions.keyPoints: Synchronous (1, 4), then Microtask (3), then Macrotask (2).

options.explanation: Synchronous code logs `1` and `4`. The microtask queue runs next (`3`), followed by the timer macrotask queue (`2`).
Async callbacks never run before synchronous code completes.
Promise microtasks run before setTimeout macrotasks.
Synchronous `4` logs before any microtasks queued during that tick.

questions.body: What are the three mutually exclusive states of a JavaScript Promise?
questions.keyPoints: Pending, Fulfilled, Rejected.

options.text: `pending`, `fulfilled`, and `rejected`
options.explanation: A Promise starts in `pending` and can transition either to `fulfilled` (with a value) or `rejected` (with a reason). Once settled, it cannot change states.

options.text: `waiting`, `resolved`, and `failed`
options.explanation: The spec terms are pending, fulfilled, and rejected.

options.text: `idle`, `running`, and `completed`
options.explanation: Those are process or thread states.

options.text: `active`, `paused`, and `stopped`
options.explanation: Not valid Promise lifecycle states.

questions.body: What happens when one promise rejects in `Promise.all` versus `Promise.allSettled`?
questions.keyPoints: Promise.all rejects immediately upon first rejection (fail-fast); Promise.allSettled waits for all to settle.

options.text: `Promise.all` immediately rejects with that rejection reason (fail-fast), while `Promise.allSettled` waits for all promises to finish and returns their outcomes.
options.explanation: `Promise.all` is fail-fast on the first rejection. `Promise.allSettled` guarantees waiting for all promises to settle and returns an array of status/value/reason objects.

options.text: Both reject immediately upon encountering the first rejected promise.
options.explanation: `Promise.allSettled` never rejects; it always resolves with an array of outcomes.

options.text: `Promise.allSettled` ignores the rejected promise and returns only fulfilled values.
options.explanation: It includes rejected outcomes as `{ status: 'rejected', reason: ... }` in the array.

options.text: `Promise.all` retries the failed promise up to 3 times automatically.
options.explanation: Native Promises do not include built-in automatic retries.

questions.body: What is the difference between `Promise.race()` and `Promise.any()`?
questions.keyPoints: Promise.race settles with the first promise to settle (fulfill or reject); Promise.any settles with the first to fulfill.

options.text: `Promise.race` settles with the first promise that settles (whether fulfilled or rejected), while `Promise.any` waits for the first promise to fulfill.
options.explanation: `Promise.race` takes the first outcome (fulfill or reject). `Promise.any` ignores rejections until one fulfills; if all reject, it rejects with an `AggregateError`.

options.text: `Promise.any` cancels all other running network requests when one resolves.
options.explanation: Promises in JS cannot be cancelled natively without `AbortController`.

options.text: `Promise.race` requires all promises to be of the same type.
options.explanation: Both accept any iterable of promises.

options.text: They are identical aliases of each other.
options.explanation: Their rejection handling semantics are fundamentally different.

questions.body: How are rejections from an `await` expression captured inside an `async` function?
questions.keyPoints: await converts a rejected promise into a thrown exception caught by try/catch.

options.text: By wrapping the `await` expression inside a standard `try...catch` block.
options.explanation: `await` unwraps rejected promises into thrown exceptions, which are caught using standard synchronous `try...catch` blocks.

options.text: By passing a callback to `await.catch()`.
options.explanation: `await` is an operator keyword, not an object with methods.

options.text: Rejections cannot be caught inside async functions.
options.explanation: Handling rejections with try/catch is the primary pattern of async/await.

options.text: By checking if the awaited variable equals `Error`.
options.explanation: A rejection throws an exception rather than returning an error object.

questions.body: What does a function declared with `async` always return?
questions.keyPoints: An async function always returns a Promise resolving to the return value.

options.text: A Promise.
options.explanation: An `async` function always returns a Promise. If a non-promise value is returned, it is automatically wrapped in `Promise.resolve()`.

options.text: The raw evaluated return value synchronously.
options.explanation: Return values are always wrapped in a Promise.

options.text: A Generator object.
options.explanation: Generators use `function*`; async functions return Promises.

options.text: `undefined` if no `await` expression was used inside the body.
options.explanation: Even without `await`, returning a value wraps it in `Promise.resolve(value)`.

questions.body:
What happens if a `.then()` handler returns a rejected promise:
```js
p.then(() => Promise.reject('error')).catch(err => ...)
```?
questions.keyPoints: Returning a rejected promise inside .then causes the returned promise to reject, routing to .catch.

options.text: The chained promise transitions to `rejected` state and passes control to the nearest downstream `.catch()` handler.
options.explanation: Returning a promise in a `.then` handler adopts its state. Returning a rejected promise forwards the rejection down the chain to the `.catch()` handler.

options.text: The rejection is treated as an uncaught exception that halts script execution.
options.explanation: The downstream `.catch()` catches it cleanly.

options.text: The chained promise remains pending indefinitely.
options.explanation: It settles immediately with rejection.

options.text: It converts the error into a fulfilled value of `'error'`.
options.explanation: Returning `Promise.reject` maintains rejection status.

questions.body: How can an in-flight `fetch()` request be programmatically cancelled in modern JavaScript?
questions.keyPoints: Pass an AbortSignal from an AbortController instance to fetch options.

options.text: By instantiating an `AbortController` and passing its `signal` into the `fetch(url, { signal })` options, then calling `controller.abort()`.
options.explanation: `AbortController` provides a `signal` property passed to `fetch`. Calling `controller.abort()` cancels the network request and rejects the promise with an `AbortError`.

options.text: By calling `fetch.cancel()` on the returned promise.
options.explanation: Native promises do not have a `.cancel()` method.

options.text: By closing the browser tab programmatically.
options.explanation: Not a valid cancellation mechanism.

options.text: By setting `window.stop()`.
options.explanation: `window.stop()` stops page loading, but `AbortController` is the granular API for fetches.

questions.body:
What is the performance difference between:
`await a(); await b();`
versus
`const p1 = a(); const p2 = b(); await Promise.all([p1, p2]);`?
questions.keyPoints: Awaiting sequentially creates a waterfall; starting promises concurrently allows parallel network execution.

options.text: The first executes sequentially (waterfall), while the second initiates both promises concurrently in parallel.
options.explanation: `await a(); await b();` waits for `a()` to finish before even invoking `b()`. Initiating both and using `Promise.all` allows both async tasks to proceed concurrently.

options.text: Both execute sequentially because JavaScript is single-threaded.
options.explanation: Underlying I/O (network/disk/timers) runs concurrently in the browser/OS.

options.text: `Promise.all` spawns two new Web Worker OS threads.
options.explanation: Promises represent asynchronous task coordination, not OS threads.

options.text: The sequential await executes faster due to V8 inline caching.
options.explanation: Sequential await takes total time = time(a) + time(b), which is slower.

questions.body: What does the browser `queueMicrotask(callback)` function do?
questions.keyPoints: Explicitly queues a microtask on the microtask queue without creating a promise.

options.text: It schedules a callback function to run on the microtask queue before the browser yields control back to the event loop macrotask queue.
options.explanation: `queueMicrotask()` provides a standardized way to schedule a microtask reliably without the overhead of creating and resolving a dummy `Promise.resolve().then()`.

options.text: It queues a task to run after the next screen repaint.
options.explanation: `requestAnimationFrame()` runs before paint; `requestIdleCallback` runs during idle time.

options.text: It creates a new background Web Worker.
options.explanation: It executes on the current JavaScript thread's microtask queue.

options.text: It runs the callback with zero-millisecond setTimeout priority.
options.explanation: Microtasks run strictly before timer macrotasks.

questions.body: Where is top-level `await` permitted in modern JavaScript without wrapping it in an `async function`?
questions.keyPoints: Top-level await is permitted at the top level of ES Modules.

options.text: At the top level of ES Modules (`<script type='module'>` or `.mjs` files).
options.explanation: Top-level `await` is an ES2022 feature supported exclusively at the top level of ECMAScript modules, allowing modules to act as async dependencies.

options.text: In any CommonJS file or classic script tag.
options.explanation: Classic scripts and CommonJS files throw `SyntaxError: await is only valid in async functions and the top level of modules`.

options.text: Inside HTML inline `onclick` attributes.
options.explanation: Inline handlers are classic script functions.

options.text: Only inside Web Worker scripts.
options.explanation: It works in standard browser and Node.js ES modules.

questions.body: What global window event is fired when a Promise rejects and has no `.catch()` rejection handler attached?
questions.keyPoints: window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection') catches uncaught promise errors.

options.text: `'unhandledrejection'`
options.explanation: When an unhandled promise rejection occurs, the browser dispatches an `unhandledrejection` event on `window` (and in Node.js on `process.on('unhandledRejection')`).

options.text: `'error'`
options.explanation: `window.onerror` handles uncaught synchronous exceptions and asset loading errors.

options.text: `'promisereject'`
options.explanation: The event name is `unhandledrejection`.

options.text: `'abort'`
options.explanation: `abort` is fired on AbortSignal instances.

questions.body: What loop syntax is used to consume asynchronous iterables returned by async generator functions (`async function*`)?
questions.keyPoints: for await (const item of asyncIterable) consumes async iterables.

options.text: `for await (const item of asyncIterable)`
options.explanation: The `for await...of` loop creates a loop iterating over async iterable objects (such as ReadableStreams or async generators), awaiting each yielded promise.

options.text: `for (const item in asyncIterable.await())`
options.explanation: `for...in` iterates over enumerable property keys.

options.text: `asyncIterable.forEachAsync(item => ...)`
options.explanation: There is no built-in `forEachAsync` method on JS iterables.

options.text: `while (asyncIterable.hasNext())`
options.explanation: Java-style `hasNext()` is not part of JS iterator protocol (which uses `.next()`).

questions.body: How do Web Workers communicate with the main browser thread without sharing memory?
questions.keyPoints: Via postMessage using the structured clone algorithm to serialize data.

options.text: Via `postMessage()` and message event handlers using the Structured Clone algorithm.
options.explanation: Web Workers run in an isolated thread with no direct DOM access. Communication occurs via `postMessage()` sending structured-cloned data across message channels.

options.text: By directly reading and writing to global variables on `window`.
options.explanation: Web Workers do not have access to `window` or DOM.

options.text: Through synchronous shared closures.
options.explanation: Threads cannot share standard JavaScript heap closures.

options.text: By polling local cookies every 50ms.
options.explanation: Message channels are event-driven and performant.

questions.body: What API allows true shared-memory concurrency between Web Workers and the main thread?
questions.keyPoints: SharedArrayBuffer with Atomics enables safe lock-free shared memory across threads.

options.text: `SharedArrayBuffer` combined with the `Atomics` object.
options.explanation: `SharedArrayBuffer` provides a shared byte buffer across workers and the main thread, while the `Atomics` namespace provides atomic operations (load, store, wait, notify) to prevent race conditions.

options.text: `LocalStorageBuffer` and `Atomics`.
options.explanation: There is no such API as LocalStorageBuffer.

options.text: `IndexedDB.transaction('shared')`.
options.explanation: IndexedDB is asynchronous disk storage, not shared in-memory buffers.

options.text: `WebSockets` with binary payload headers.
options.explanation: WebSockets are network protocols, not local thread-memory APIs.

questions.body: What arguments does a `Promise.prototype.finally(callback)` callback receive, and what does it return?
questions.keyPoints: finally callback receives zero arguments and passes through the previous settled value/reason unless it throws.

options.text: It receives no arguments (`0` args), and passes through the prior fulfilled value or rejection reason unless the callback throws or returns a rejected promise.
options.explanation: `.finally()` is executed regardless of fulfillment or rejection without receiving the outcome, transparently preserving the preceding promise settlement.

options.text: It receives `(error, result)` like Node.js callbacks.
options.explanation: `.finally()` takes a zero-argument callback.

options.text: It always overrides the resolved value with `undefined`.
options.explanation: It transparently passes through the original resolved value.

options.text: It only executes if the promise rejected.
options.explanation: It executes on both fulfillment and rejection.

questions.body: What happens if a recursive microtask loop is created (e.g. `function loop() { Promise.resolve().then(loop); } loop();`)?
questions.keyPoints: The microtask queue will continuously replenish, starving the macrotask queue and freezing the UI.

options.text: The event loop continuously drains microtasks and never moves to macrotasks or UI rendering, freezing the web page.
options.explanation: The event loop drains the microtask queue completely before rendering or running macrotasks. Recursively queuing microtasks causes microtask starvation and hangs the UI.

options.text: The browser automatically caps microtasks at 1000 and drops the rest.
options.explanation: The browser does not discard microtasks; it freezes until an out-of-memory or unresponsive script prompt appears.

options.text: It throws a `MaximumCallStackSizeExceeded` error immediately.
options.explanation: Stack frames unwind between microtask resolutions; the call stack does not overflow, the queue simply never empties.

options.text: The microtasks are automatically downgraded to setTimeout macrotasks.
options.explanation: Microtasks maintain microtask priority.

questions.body: In front-end performance, what is the core behavioral difference between a debounced function and a throttled function?
questions.keyPoints: Debounce delays execution until a quiet period of N ms; throttle guarantees execution at most once every N ms.

options.text: Debouncing delays execution until `N` ms have passed since the LAST event, while Throttling guarantees execution at most once every `N` ms during continuous events.
options.explanation: Debounce waits for silence (ideal for search input auto-complete). Throttle guarantees periodic execution at a fixed interval (ideal for window scroll/resize events).

options.text: Throttling delays execution until events stop; debouncing executes on every tick.
options.explanation: The definitions are reversed.

options.text: Debouncing uses Web Workers; throttling uses CSS transitions.
options.explanation: Both are pure JavaScript timer/timestamp rate-limiting techniques.

options.text: Debouncing can only handle keyboard inputs; throttling only handles mouse events.
options.explanation: Both can be applied to any recurring event or function call.

questions.body: What is the correct syntax for an async Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE)?
questions.keyPoints: (async () => { await ... })();

options.text: `(async () => { /* await something */ })();`
options.explanation: Placing `async` before parameter parentheses of the IIFE creates an async function invoked immediately via trailing `()`.

options.text: `async ({ /* await something */ })();`
options.explanation: Missing function declaration syntax.

options.text: `await (() => { /* something */ })();`
options.explanation: Cannot use await outside an async function or module top-level.

options.text: `(() => async { /* something */ })();`
options.explanation: `async` must precede parameter list, not body braces.
